cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK III
Pylos: Nestor's tales of the returns;\nTelemachus rides for Sparta.
And the sun leapt up, leaving the beautiful water,\ninto the bronze-bright heaven, to shine for the immortals
and for mortal men across the grain-giving plowland;
and they came in to Pylos,\nthe strong-built city of Neleus.
There on the beach of the sea\nthe people were offering victims,
bulls all black, to the earth-shaker\nwith the blue-black hair.
Nine tiers of seats there were,\nfive hundred sitting in each,
and before each company nine bulls were held ready.
They had just tasted the innards,\nand were burning thigh-cuts for the god,
when the ship came straight in:\nthey brailed the sails of the trim vessel,
furled them aloft, moored her,\nand stepped ashore themselves;
and Telemachus stepped from the ship,\nAthena going before him.
The goddess spoke to him first, gray-eyed Athena:
"Telemachus, no more need of\nshyness now, not a scrap of it:
this is why you have sailed the sea — to learn news
of your father: where the earth\nhides him, what doom he met.
Come then, go straight to Nestor, breaker of horses:
let us see what counsel he keeps hidden in his breast.
Beg him yourself, so that he speaks unerring truth.
He will tell you no lie:\nhe is clear-headed beyond most men."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered her:
"Mentor, how am I to go up? How greet him?
I have no practice yet in close-woven speech —\nand a young man is shy of questioning his elder."
Then the goddess spoke to him again, gray-eyed Athena:
"Telemachus, some of it your own heart will see,\nand some a god will prompt. For I do not think
you were born and raised without the gods' good will."
So speaking, Pallas Athena led the way swiftly,\nand he followed in the footsteps of the god.
They came to the gathering-place of\nthe men of Pylos, the rows of seats,
where Nestor sat with his sons, and around them companions
were readying the feast,\nroasting meats and skewering others.
But when they saw the strangers they came all in a crowd,
clasped their hands in welcome, and bade them be seated.
First Peisistratus, Nestor's son, coming near,\ntook the hands of both, and settled them at the feast
on soft fleeces over the sand of the sea,\nbeside his brother Thrasymedes and his father;
and he gave them portions of the innards, and poured\nwine into a golden cup, and pledging her he addressed
Pallas Athena, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus:
"Pray now, stranger, to the lord Poseidon,\nfor his is the feast you have found in coming here.
And when you have poured and prayed, as is right and\ncustom, give this man too the cup of honey-sweet wine
to pour, since he also, I think,\nprays to the deathless ones:
all men have need of the gods.
But he is the younger, my own age to the year,\nand so to you first I give the golden cup."
With that he set in her hand the cup of sweet wine;\nand Athena rejoiced in the man — clear-headed, just —
because to her first he gave the golden cup;\nand at once she prayed at length to the lord Poseidon:
"Hear me, Poseidon who hold the earth, and do not\ngrudge us who pray the accomplishment of these works.
To Nestor first of all, and to his sons, grant glory,\nand then to all the rest give gracious recompense,
to all the Pylians, for this splendid hecatomb.
And grant besides that Telemachus and\nI sail home with the thing accomplished
we came here for, in our fast black ship."
So she prayed — and she herself was accomplishing it all.
Then she gave Telemachus the beautiful two-handled cup,\nand the dear son of Odysseus prayed the same.
And when they had roasted the\nouter meats and drawn them off,
they divided the portions and feasted the glorious feast.
But when they had put away desire for food and drink,
Gerenian Nestor the horseman began to speak among them:
"Now is the fairer time to inquire and ask our guests\nwho they are, now they have had their joy of food.
Strangers, who are you?\nFrom where do you sail the watery ways?
Is it on some business — or do you rove at\nrandom, the way sea-raiders do, who wander
staking their own lives, bearing evil to strangers?"
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him, emboldened:\nAthena herself had set courage in his heart,
so that he might ask about his absent father\nand so that good report among men might be his:
"Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Achaeans,\nyou ask from where we are, and I will tell you.
We have come from Ithaca, under Mount Neion;\nand the business I speak of is private, not the people's.
I follow the wide fame of my father,\nin hope I may hear of him:
noble, enduring-hearted Odysseus, who once, they say,\nfought at your side when you sacked the Trojans' city.
All the others, all who warred against the Trojans,
we have had word of —\nwhere each man died his bitter death;
but his death the son of Cronos has left past finding:
no one can say for certain where he perished,\nwhether he went down on the mainland at enemy hands
or on the deep, under the waves of Amphitrite.
That is why I come now to your knees: in hope you will\nconsent to tell his bitter death — whether you saw it
with your own eyes, or heard the tale of him from another
wanderer. Beyond all men his mother bore him for sorrow.
Do not soften anything from courtesy or pity:
tell me fully whatever sight you came upon.
I beg you — if ever my father, good Odysseus,\npromised you word or work and made it good
in the Trojans' country,\nwhere you Achaeans suffered your pains,
remember it for me now: tell me the unerring truth."
Then Gerenian Nestor the horseman answered him:
"Dear boy — since you bring back the misery we endured\nin that country, we headstrong sons of the Achaeans,
all our roving in ships across the misted\nsea chasing plunder wherever Achilles led,
and all our fighting around the great city of lord Priam —\nthere, in those years, our best were killed.
There lies Ajax, dear to the war-god; there Achilles;\nthere Patroclus, a counselor the equal of the gods;
there my own dear son, strong and without fault,\nAntilochus — surpassing swift of foot, and a fighter.
And many other evils we suffered besides:\nwho among mortal men could tell them all?
Not if you stayed five years — six years —\nasking all the evils the noble Achaeans suffered there:
you would go home to your own country worn out first.
Nine years we stitched evils around them, plotting
with every kind of cunning — and the son\nof Cronos barely brought it to an end.
And there no man would set his wits against him openly —\nwilling, that is — for noble Odysseus won by far,
in every kind of cunning: your father — if truly\nyou are his blood. Awe takes me, looking at you.
Your speech, at least, is his: you would not\nthink a younger man could speak so like him.
In all that time, I and noble Odysseus never\nspoke on opposite sides in assembly or in council:
one heart between us — with sense and considered counsel
we planned for the Argives how the best might come about.
But when we had sacked Priam's steep city,\nand gone to our ships, and a god scattered the Achaeans,
then, then Zeus devised in his heart a bitter homecoming
for the Argives — since not all of us were men of sense\nor of justice. So many of them came to an evil end
through the ruinous wrath of the\ngray-eyed daughter of the mighty Father —
who set strife between the two sons of Atreus.
The two of them called the Achaeans all to assembly —\nrashly, in no due order, at the setting of the sun,
and the sons of the Achaeans came heavy with wine —
and they spoke out the reason they had gathered the army.
There Menelaus urged all the Achaeans to remember\nhomecoming across the broad back of the sea;
and it did not please Agamemnon, not at all:\nhe wanted to hold the army back, and offer holy hecatombs
to heal the terrible anger of Athena — the fool.\nHe did not know she was not to be persuaded:
the mind of the gods who are\nforever does not turn so fast.
So the two of them stood trading hard words;\nand the strong-greaved Achaeans sprang up
with a huge din, and the counsel split them two ways.
That night we lay on our anger, brooding hard thoughts
against each other — for Zeus\nwas readying the stroke of evil —
and at dawn half of us hauled our\nships to the bright salt water
and loaded our goods aboard, and the deep-girdled women.
Half the army held back, staying there with\nAtreus' son Agamemnon, shepherd of the people;
and half of us embarked and rowed. And the ships ran fast,
for a god smoothed the sea over its monstrous deeps.
Coming to Tenedos, we offered victims to the gods,
aching for home. But Zeus had\nno thought yet of homecoming —
iron-hearted, he stirred up evil strife a second time.
Some turned their curved ships around and went back —
those with Odysseus, the battle-wise lord,\nthe man of shifting counsels —
carrying favor once again to Atreus' son Agamemnon.
But I, with the ships that followed me gathered close,\nfled on, for I knew the god was devising evils.
And the warlike son of Tydeus fled,\nand roused his companions.
Late upon our track came fair-haired Menelaus,\nand caught us at Lesbos debating the long crossing:
whether to sail above rugged Chios,\nby the isle of Psyria, keeping Chios on our left,
or under Chios, past windy Mimas.
We asked the god to show a sign, and he showed one,\nand bade us cut across the middle sea to Euboea,
to run out from under the evil quickest.
A whistling wind sprang up astern, and the ships\nran fast down the fish-filled ways, and to Geraestus
they came in by night. And to Poseidon we laid many
bulls' thighs on the fire, having measured the great gulf.
It was the fourth day when in Argos the companions of\nDiomedes, breaker of horses, moored their trim ships;
but I held on for Pylos, and the wind never\nfailed from the day the god first sent it blowing.
So I came home, dear child,\nknowing nothing — I cannot tell you
who of the Achaeans were saved and who were lost.
But all I hear, sitting here in our halls,\nyou shall learn, as is right; I will hide nothing.
The Myrmidons, they say,\nthose furious spearmen, came home safe,
led by the shining son of great-hearted Achilles;\nsafe too Philoctetes, Poias' splendid son;
and Idomeneus brought all his companions to Crete,\nall who escaped the war: the sea took none from him.
And Atreus' son — you have heard\nyourselves, far off as you live,
how he came home, and how\nAegisthus plotted his bitter death.
But that man paid for it — grimly, in full.
How good a thing it is,\nthat a son of the dead man be left!
For that son took vengeance on the killer of his father,
Aegisthus of the crooked counsels,\nwho cut down his famous father.
You too, my friend — and I see how tall and fine you are —
be brave, so that men not yet\nborn will speak well of you."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Achaeans,
yes — that man took his vengeance\nin full, and the Achaeans
will carry his fame wide,\na thing for men to come to hear of.
If only the gods would clothe me in strength like that,\nto pay the suitors back for their galling trespass —
the insolent men who scheme their\nreckless outrage against me!
But the gods have spun no such happiness for me —
not for my father, not for me.\nNow, come what may, I must endure."
Then Gerenian Nestor the horseman answered him:
"Dear boy — since you say it\nyourself and bring it to my mind —
they tell me many suitors for your mother's sake\nfill your halls against your will, devising evils.
Tell me: do you bow to it willingly, or do the people
through the land hate you, following the voice of a god?
Who knows whether one day he will\ncome and repay their violence —
alone, it may be, or all the Achaeans with him?
If only gray-eyed Athena chose to love you the\nway she cared in those days for glorious Odysseus
in the Trojans' country,\nwhere we Achaeans suffered our pains —
never have I seen the gods love a man so openly\nas Pallas Athena stood by him, in the open —
if she chose to love you like that,\nand care for you in her heart,
then more than one of those men would\nforget about marriage for good."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Old sir, I do not think that\nword will ever be accomplished.
What you say is too great. Awe holds me. I could not
hope for it to happen —\nnot if the gods themselves willed it."
Then the goddess spoke to him again, gray-eyed Athena:
"Telemachus, what a word has\nslipped the fence of your teeth!
Easily, if he wills it, a god brings\na man safe home — even from far away.
And I would rather suffer pains in plenty first and\nthen come home, and look on my day of homecoming,
than come and die at my own hearth, as Agamemnon died,\nby the treachery of Aegisthus and of his own wife.
But death — the death common to all — not even the gods
can beat away from a man they love, once the day comes
when the ruinous doom of death\nthat lays men low takes hold."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered her:
"Mentor, let us speak of it no\nlonger, grieved though we are.
For him no homecoming is real any more: long since the\ndeathless ones have plotted his death and black doom.
Now there is another word I want to ask, of Nestor —\nsince beyond other men he knows judgments and wisdom;
three generations of men, they say, he has ruled as king,
and to my eyes he seems like one of the deathless ones.
Nestor, son of Neleus: tell me the truth of it —\nhow did Atreus' son die, wide-ruling Agamemnon?
Where was Menelaus? What death\ndid the schemer plot for him,
Aegisthus of the crooked counsels —\nsince the man he killed was far the better?
Was Menelaus not in Achaean Argos — was he wandering
somewhere among men, that the\nother took heart and killed?"
Then Gerenian Nestor the horseman answered him:
"Then I will tell you, child, the whole truth of it.
You have guessed yourself how it would have gone,\nif Atreus' son, fair-haired Menelaus, coming from Troy,
had found Aegisthus alive in the halls:
no man would have heaped the mounded earth over\nhis dead body — dogs and birds would have torn him
as he lay on the plain far from the city, and not one
of the Achaean women would have wept him:\ntoo monstrous the thing he schemed.
For we were over there, winning our many contests —\nand he, at his ease in a fold of horse-grazing Argos,
worked all the while at Agamemnon's\nwife with charming words.
At first she pushed the shameful thing away —\nshining Clytemnestra — for her mind was still sound;
and beside her, too, there was a singer, whom Atreus' son
strictly charged, when he left\nfor Troy, to guard his wife.
But when the doom of the gods bound her to her undoing,\nthen Aegisthus led that singer to a desert island
and left him there, spoil and carrion for the birds,
and led her — he willing,\nshe willing — home to his own house.
Many thigh-cuts he burned on the gods' holy altars,\nmany offerings he hung up, woven things and gold,
having accomplished the enormity\nhis heart had never hoped for.
Now we had sailed together on the way from Troy,\nAtreus' son and I, in all friendship;
but when we reached holy Sunium, the headland of Athens,\nthere Phoebus Apollo came with his gentle arrows
and killed the helmsman of Menelaus,\nthe steering-oar of the running ship still in his hands:
Phrontis, Onetor's son, who outdid all the tribes of\nmen at steering a ship when the storm-winds drive.
So Menelaus was held there,\npressed though he was for the road,
to bury his companion and pay the death-rites over him.
But when he too, going on over the wine-dark sea in\nthe hollow ships, came at a run to the steep height
of Malea, then wide-voiced Zeus devised for him a\nhateful road: he poured on the breath of screaming winds
and monstrous waves, swollen huge as mountains.
There he split the fleet, and part he drove on Crete,
where the Cydonians lived around the streams of Iardanus.
There is a bare cliff, sheer to the salt water,\nat the edge of Gortyn on the misted sea,
where the South Wind shoves the\ngreat swell on the left headland,
toward Phaestus, and a little\nstone holds back the great sea.
There part of them came in,\nand the men escaped destruction
barely, but the waves smashed the ships on the reefs;\nand the other five ships with their dark-blue prows
the wind and the water carried and beached on Egypt.
So Menelaus, gathering much substance and gold,\nroved with his ships among men of alien speech —
and in that very time Aegisthus\nschemed those horrors at home.
Seven years he reigned over Mycenae rich in gold,
having killed Atreus' son,\nand the people were broken under him;
but in the eighth his evil came on him: noble Orestes,\nback from Athens, cut down his father's killer —
Aegisthus of the crooked counsels,\nwho cut down his famous father.
The killing done, he gave the Argives a funeral feast\nfor his hateful mother and for spineless Aegisthus;
and on that same day Menelaus of\nthe great war-cry reached him,
bringing home treasure,\nall the freight his ships could bear.
You too, my friend: do not wander long and far from home,\nleaving your goods behind and men in your house
of such overbearing insolence —\nor they will devour it all,
dividing your goods among them,\nand your journey come to nothing.
But to Menelaus I bid you go — I urge it:
he is newly home from foreign parts,\nfrom among peoples no man would hope in his heart
to return from, once the storm-winds had driven him\nastray into a sea so vast that not even the birds
can cross it in a year — so vast it is, and terrible.
Go now, with your own ship and your companions;
or if you would rather go by land,\nchariot and horses are here,
and here are my sons, who will be your escorts to\nshining Lacedaemon, where fair-haired Menelaus is.
Beg him yourself, so that he speaks unerring truth.
He will tell you no lie:\nhe is clear-headed beyond most men."
So he spoke; and the sun went down, and the dusk came on.
And among them spoke the goddess, gray-eyed Athena:
"Old sir, all this you have told rightly, in due measure.
But come — cut up the tongues now, and mix the wine,\nso that we may pour to Poseidon and the other immortals
and then think of sleep. It is the hour for it:
the light is gone already under the\nwestern gloom, and it is not fitting
to sit long at the feast of the gods, but to go home."
So spoke the daughter of Zeus, and they heard her voice.
Heralds poured water over their hands,\nand young men crowned the mixing-bowls with drink
and served all, pouring first\ndrops in each cup for the gods;
and they threw the tongues in the fire,\nand stood, and poured above them.
But when they had poured, and drunk what their\nhearts would have, then Athena and godlike Telemachus
both made to go back to the hollow ship.
But Nestor held them back,\ncatching at them with his words:
"Zeus forbid it — and the other deathless gods —\nthat you should go from my house to your fast ship
as if from some man utterly cloakless and poor,\nwho has no cloaks, no plenty of blankets in his house,
no soft sleeping for himself or for his guests!
I have cloaks and beautiful blankets in plenty.
Never, while I live, shall the dear son of this man\nOdysseus lie down on a ship's deck-planks — nor after,
while sons of mine are left in the halls to\nhost whatever guest arrives at my doors."
Then the goddess spoke to him again, gray-eyed Athena:
"Well said, dear old friend — and it is fitting\nthat Telemachus obey you: far better so.
Let him go with you now, then, and sleep in\nyour halls. But I will go to the black ship
to hearten the companions and give them all their orders.
For I may claim to be the only elder among them:
the rest are younger men who follow out of friendship,\nall of an age with great-hearted Telemachus.
There let me lie down tonight, by the black hollow ship;
and in the morning I go on to the great-hearted\nCauconians, where a debt is owed me — no new thing
and no small one. But this man,\nsince he has come to your house,
send on with a chariot and a son of yours; and give\nhim horses, your lightest runners, your strongest."
So speaking, gray-eyed Athena went away in the likeness\nof a sea-eagle; and amazement took all who saw,
and the old man marveled, when his eyes had seen it.
He took Telemachus' hand, and spoke a word, and named him:
"Dear friend, I have no fear you\nwill prove base or spineless,
if the gods walk with you so, escorts, and you so young!
For this was none other of those who hold Olympus\nthan the daughter of Zeus, most glorious Tritogeneia,
she who honored your noble father too among the Argives.
Queen, be gracious! Grant me good fame —\nto me, to my children, to my honored wife —
and I in turn will offer you a\nyearling heifer, broad of brow,
unbroken, that no man has ever led under the yoke:
her I will offer to you,\nwith gold poured round her horns."
So he spoke in prayer, and Pallas Athena heard him.
Then Gerenian Nestor the horseman led them — his sons\nand his daughters' husbands — to his beautiful house.
And when they reached the lord's famous house,\nthey sat in order on the benches and the high-backed chairs,
and for their coming the old man mixed a bowl\nof sweet-drinking wine, eleven years old,
which the woman-steward opened, loosening the sealing cap.
Of this the old man mixed a bowl, and to Athena
he prayed long, pouring,\nto the daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus.
But when they had poured,\nand drunk what their hearts would have,
the others went home to sleep, each man to his own house,
but Gerenian Nestor the horseman laid him down there —\nTelemachus, dear son of godlike Odysseus —
on a corded bedstead under the echoing porch,
and beside him Peisistratus of the good ash spear,\nleader of men, the one son in his halls still unwed;
and he himself slept in the inner room of the high house,
where the lady his wife made ready his bed and his rest.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,\nGerenian Nestor the horseman rose up from his bed,
and came out, and took his seat on the polished\nstones that stood before his high doors,
white, gleaming as if with oil. On these, in the old days,
Neleus used to sit, a counselor the equal of the gods;
but he long since had gone down to Hades, broken by fate,
and now Gerenian Nestor sat there\nin his turn, warder of the Achaeans,
holding the scepter. Around him\nhis sons gathered in a body,
coming from their rooms: Echephron and Stratius,\nPerseus and Aretus and godlike Thrasymedes;
and sixth came the hero Peisistratus to join them,
and they led godlike Telemachus\nand seated him beside them.
And Gerenian Nestor the horseman\nbegan to speak among them:
"Quickly, dear children, work my wish for me,\nso that first of all the gods I may propitiate Athena,
who came to me in visible\npresence at the god's rich feast.
Come then: one of you to the plain for a heifer,\nfast as may be, and let the cowherd drive her in;
one go down to great-hearted Telemachus' black ship\nand bring up all his companions — leave two men only;
one bid the goldsmith Laerces come here\nto pour gold round the heifer's horns.
The rest of you stay here together;\nand tell the slave-women
inside to make ready a feast through the famous house —\nseats, and firewood round about, and shining water."
So he spoke, and they all fell to bustling. The heifer\ncame up from the plain; from the fast trim ship came
great-hearted Telemachus' companions; the smith came
with his bronze tools in his hands,\nthe instruments of his art,
anvil and hammer and the well-made fire-tongs\nhe worked the gold with; and Athena came
to receive her offering. And the old horseman Nestor\ngave gold, and the smith worked it and poured it round
the heifer's horns, so the goddess\nmight see the glory and be glad.
Stratius and noble Echephron led her by the horns;\nAretus came from the storeroom carrying lustral water
in a flowered basin, and in his\nother hand the barley-grains
in a basket; and Thrasymedes,\nsteadfast in battle, stood by
with a sharp axe in his hand, to strike the heifer down;
Perseus held the blood-bowl. And the old horseman Nestor
began with the hand-water and the\nbarley-grains, and long to Athena
he prayed, making first offering,\ncasting hairs from the head into the fire.
And when they had prayed and thrown the scattering barley,
straightway Nestor's son, high-spirited Thrasymedes,\nstood close and struck: the axe cut through the tendons
of the neck, and undid the heifer's\nstrength. And the women cried aloud —
the daughters and the sons' wives and the honored wife
of Nestor, Eurydice, eldest of the daughters of Clymenus.
Then the men lifted her up from the wide-wayed earth
and held her, and Peisistratus,\nleader of men, cut the throat.
And when the black blood had run out,\nand the life had left the bones,
quickly they broke her apart,\nand at once cut out the thigh-pieces
all in due order, and wrapped them deep in fat,\nfolding it double, and laid raw flesh upon them.
The old man burned them on the split wood,\nand poured the fire-bright wine
over; and the young men beside\nhim held the five-tined forks.
And when the thighs were burned through,\nand they had tasted the innards,
they carved up the rest and threaded it on spits and\nroasted it, holding the sharp spits in their hands.
Meanwhile beautiful Polycaste had bathed Telemachus —\nthe youngest daughter of Nestor, Neleus' son.
And when she had bathed him\nand rubbed him richly with oil,
she threw a beautiful mantle around him, and a tunic,
and he stepped from the bath with the body of an immortal,
and went and sat down beside Nestor,\nshepherd of the people.
And when they had roasted the\nouter meats and drawn them off,
they sat and feasted; and good men waited\non them, pouring wine into cups of gold.
But when they had put away desire for food and drink,
Gerenian Nestor the horseman began to speak among them:
"My sons, come — yoke the\nfine-maned horses for Telemachus,
lead them under the chariot, so he may be making his way."
So he spoke, and they listened well and obeyed:
quickly they yoked the swift horses under the chariot,\nand the woman-steward put in bread and wine
and cooked meats, such things as Zeus-nurtured kings eat.
Then Telemachus mounted the beautiful chariot,\nand beside him Peisistratus, Nestor's son, leader of men,
mounted the chariot and took the reins in his hands,
and whipped them to a run;\nand the pair flew on, nothing loath,
into the plain, and left the steep city of Pylos behind.
All day long they shook the yoke they bore between them.
The sun went down, and all the ways grew dark,\nand they came to Pherae, to the house of Diocles,
son of Ortilochus, whom Alpheus fathered.
There they slept the night,\nand he set guest-gifts before them.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,
they yoked the horses and mounted the inlaid chariot\nand drove out of the gateway and the echoing porch;
and he whipped them to a run,\nand the pair flew on, nothing loath.
They came to the wheat-bearing\nplain, and there they pressed
to the journey's end: so well\nthe swift horses carried them.
The sun went down, and all the ways grew dark.
